title: The Rope Bridge Between Yesterdays
summary: A rope bridge in the gorge above Mistmoor crosses not to the other side, but to yesterday. Emet crosses it to undo the careless word that lost him his best friend — and learns that the bridge charges a toll, and that you cannot change the past without unmaking who the past made you.

chapters.title: The Bridge in the Gorge
chapters.body:
Above the village of Mistmoor there was a gorge, and across the gorge there was a rope bridge, and the rope bridge did not go where bridges usually go.

It did not cross to the other side of the gorge. Oh, it looked as though it did — you could see the far cliff through the drifting mist, with the bridge running out toward it. But everyone in Mistmoor knew the truth, passed down in careful warnings: if you walked all the way across that bridge, you did not arrive at the far cliff. You arrived at yesterday. The bridge crossed time, not space. Step onto it today, walk to the far end, and you'd step off into the world exactly as it had been one day before.

And nobody used it. That was the strange thing. A bridge to yesterday sounds like a marvel, a gift, a thing people would line up to cross. But the elders of Mistmoor forbade it, and made sure the children understood, and the bridge stood empty year after year, swaying in the mist, because — the elders said — there was a toll, and the toll was too high, and those who crossed to change a yesterday never came back the same, if they came back at all.

Emet was twelve, and he had a yesterday he would have given anything to change.

His best friend was named Pel, and they had been friends since before either could remember — the kind of friendship that feels less like something you have and more like something you're made of. And three days ago, Emet had ruined it. There had been a silly quarrel, the sort friends have, and Emet had lost his temper, and said the cruelest thing he could think of — a true thing, a secret thing Pel had told him in trust, thrown back in Pel's face to wound him. He'd seen it land. He'd seen Pel's face change. And Pel had walked away and not spoken to him since, and when Emet tried to apologize, Pel wouldn't look at him, because some words can't be unsaid, and Emet had said one.

Emet couldn't bear it. The careless cruel word sat in his chest like a stone, and he replayed the moment a hundred times a day, wishing with his whole soul that he could take it back, that he could go back to before he said it and just... not say it. Just keep his mouth shut. Change that one moment, and have his friend back.

And there was a bridge, above the village, that crossed to yesterday.

Emet knew he wasn't supposed to. He knew the elders forbade it, knew there was a toll. But he also knew that his friendship — the thing he was half made of — was lying broken because of one word, and here was a bridge that could take him back to unsay it. So one grey morning, before the village woke, Emet climbed up to the gorge, and stood at the near end of the rope bridge to yesterday, and looked out across it into the drifting mist.

And he stepped onto the bridge.

chapters.title: The Toll
chapters.body:
The bridge swayed under Emet's feet, and the mist closed around him, and as he walked he began to understand that this was no ordinary crossing.

With each step toward yesterday, he felt something being drawn out of him. Not memories, exactly — something deeper. At the first plank, he felt a wave of the last three days lift away: the misery of losing Pel, the hundred replayings of the cruel word, the aching regret. It simply... thinned, and faded, as if he were walking backward out of it. And that was almost a relief, at first. But it kept going. With each plank, more of him was drawn out into the mist — not just the pain of the last three days, but the learning in it. The thing he had come to understand, over three miserable days, about what his cruel word had cost, and why he must never do such a thing again. That understanding — hard-won, paid for in three days of guilt — was being pulled out of him plank by plank, unlearned, erased, as he walked back toward the moment before he'd learned it.

Halfway across, Emet stopped, swaying in the mist, and understood the toll at last.

The bridge would take him back to yesterday — to the moment before he said the cruel word. He could unsay it. He could have his friend back, the quarrel un-had, the word unspoken. But the toll was this: he would arrive back there as the boy he had been before he said it. Which meant he would arrive without any of what he'd learned by saying it. All the understanding he'd gained in three days of regret — about how much a careless word can wound, about what his friendship was worth, about the kind of person he wanted to be and the kind he didn't — all of it would be gone, drawn out into the mist, the price of the crossing. He would step off the bridge into yesterday exactly as ignorant, exactly as careless, exactly as capable of cruelty as he'd been the moment before he learned better.

And Emet realized, with a slow cold dread, what that meant. If he arrived back in yesterday having unlearned everything the mistake had taught him — then he would be, once again, a boy who didn't yet know how much a cruel word could cost. A boy just as likely to lose his temper and say the cruel thing all over again. He might unsay this word, only to say another. Because the only thing that had taught him not to be cruel was the cruelty itself, and its cost, and the bridge was charging him exactly that lesson as its toll. He could undo the wound, but only by unmaking the person the wound had taught him to become.

He stood swaying in the middle of the bridge, halfway between today and yesterday, and he saw the whole shape of it. This was why the elders forbade the crossing. This was the toll too high to pay. You could go back and change a yesterday — but you had to leave behind, in the mist, everything that yesterday had taught you. And so you never really fixed your mistake. You just erased the you that had learned from it, and sent back in your place a you doomed to make it again, having learned nothing. A person who un-lives their regrets un-lives their growing, too. The two cannot be separated. They are the same planks of the same bridge.

Behind him lay today — the broken friendship, the aching regret, but also everything he'd learned. Ahead lay yesterday — the friendship whole, but himself unmade, ignorant again, the lesson wiped away. And Emet had to choose which way to walk.

chapters.title: The Way Back
chapters.body:
Emet stood in the middle of the rope bridge for a long time, in the drifting mist, halfway between the yesterday he wanted and the today he'd learned in.

He thought about walking on. About stepping off into yesterday, into the moment before the quarrel, and simply not saying the cruel word — having his friend back, whole, the wound never made. It pulled at him so hard. Pel's face, un-hurt. The friendship, unbroken. All he had to do was keep walking.

But he made himself think it all the way through, the way he was only able to because he hadn't finished crossing yet — because he still, for now, had the understanding the bridge hadn't finished taking. If he walked on, he'd arrive in yesterday as a boy who'd never learned what cruelty costs. And that boy — he knew it now, he could see it clearly — that boy would quarrel again, and lose his temper again, and probably say something cruel again, because nothing would have taught him not to. He'd be trading a wound he'd learned from for the same wound waiting to happen again, this time with no lesson at the end of it. He wouldn't be saving the friendship. He'd just be setting it up to break the same way, over and over, each time erasing the boy who might have finally learned better.

And there was something worse, something he felt in his chest as he stood there. The regret he was carrying — the stone of it, the misery of the cruel word replayed a hundred times — that regret was awful. But it was also the most honest thing he had. It was proof that he understood what he'd done. It was the shape of him becoming someone who wouldn't do it again. If he walked on and let the mist take it, he wouldn't just lose the pain. He'd lose the person the pain was making him into. And that person — the one who understood, the one who'd learned, the one who would never throw a friend's secret in their face again — that was the person Pel deserved as a friend. Not the careless boy from before. The one who'd learned better.

So Emet turned around.

It was the hardest thing he had ever done, turning his back on the yesterday where his friend still loved him. But he did it. And he walked back the way he'd come — and with each plank toward today, he felt the toll returning to him, given back: the regret flowing back into his chest, the understanding returning, the hard-won lesson settling back where it belonged. By the time he stepped off the bridge onto solid today, he had all of it again — the broken friendship, the aching guilt, and every painful thing he'd learned. He was himself again, whole, mistake and lesson and all.

He walked down into the village, and he went to find Pel.

He couldn't unsay the cruel word. That was real now, permanently, and no bridge would erase it without erasing him. But he could do the other thing — the harder, truer thing. He could apologize as the boy who had actually learned. Not to undo the wound, but to own it.

He found Pel by the well, and this time Emet didn't make excuses, didn't ask to be forgiven quickly, didn't try to make it as though it hadn't happened. He just told the truth. "I said the cruelest thing I could think of, and I used something you trusted me with to do it, and it was wrong, and I've thought about it every hour since, and I understand now how badly it hurt you, and I'm not asking you to pretend it didn't happen. I just needed you to know that I know. And that I'm so sorry. And that I'll never, ever do it again — not because I forgot how it felt, but because I'll always remember."

And Pel looked at him — really looked at him, for the first time in three days. Because there is a difference, and Pel could feel it, between an apology that wants to erase a wrong and an apology that has truly understood it. The first asks you to forget. The second earns its way back. And Emet's was the second kind — the kind that could only come from a boy who had carried his regret instead of erasing it, and been changed by it.

It did not fix everything at once. Trust, once cracked, mends slowly, like the gold-seamed cups of another town. But it began to mend — truly mend, the honest way — because Emet had come back not as the boy who'd never wounded Pel, but as the boy who had, and had learned, and had chosen to carry it.

They were friends again, in time. A different kind of friends — a little more careful with each other, a little more honest, the friendship gold-seamed now where it had cracked. And Emet never crossed the bridge in the gorge, not then and not ever, though he understood now why it was so tempting and why it was forbidden. Because he had learned the thing the elders had always known: that you cannot change your yesterdays without unmaking the person your yesterdays have made you. And the person your mistakes make you — the one who has learned, and grown, and carries what they've done — is the only person who can actually make tomorrow better. Erase the regret, and you erase the growing. Carry it, and you become someone who won't need to.
